text: Government House is the official residence of the lieutenant governor of Jersey and is located in the parish of St Saviour. It serves as a venue for ceremonial functions, receptions, and meetings with visiting foreign dignitaries and heads of state, and also functions as the official residence of the Duke of Normandy (currently King Charles III) when he is in Jersey. The current building is at least the fifth official residence of governors and lieutenant governors of Jersey. Early governors or their lieutenants lived at Mont Orgueil and later at Elizabeth Castle, though the latter’s status as a tidal island led to a preference for accommodation in Saint Helier. In 1727, Colonel Magnus Kempenfelt resided in a house belonging to Le Geyt. During the Battle of Jersey in 1781, Major Moise Corbet lived at Le Manoir de la Motte, where he was captured by French invaders. Around 1800, under General Andrew Gordon, a house adjacent to the Royal Square was acquired and described in 1809 as a "large, substantial and commodious stone mansion with appropriate offices, pleasure and kitchen gardens". Under General Sir George Don, offices for public business were added, but Major-General Sir Colin Halkett petitioned the British Government in 1821 to exchange this town-centre property due to expensive repair needs, susceptibility to flooding from Le Grand Douet, and inadequate suitability for public entertainment. In 1803, the rector of St Saviour's Church, Rev. Philip Le Breton, purchased the land where Government House now stands and built a family home. This was bought by shipowner François Janvrin in 1814, who demolished the house and constructed a small two-storey villa named Belmont, using mahogany imported from South America, including for the main staircase, which remains a notable feature. In 1822, Major-General Sir Colin Halkett, then lieutenant governor, exchanged the old Government House in Saint Helier and Le Pré au Roi in Saint Clement for the Belmont property and additional land, after which it has been the official residence of all subsequent lieutenant governors. Halkett had noted that the lieutenant governor would have the opportunity at Belmont to host inhabitants and strangers without apparent bias, but his ADC, John Le Couteur, criticized the property, stating the masonry was "shamefully done". A guardhouse was built at the time for £215, though the house was considered unprepossessing. Projects to add a third storey were considered but not implemented until the second half of the 19th century, with further improvements including the addition of a porte-cochère. The drive was formerly part of La Ruette du Sacrement, leading to St Saviour's Church, and was purchased in 1810, later replaced by the new military road (St Saviour's Hill or Lé Mont du Gouvèrneux). The 12-acre grounds, situated in a valley setting from the formal lawns, include an ornamental lake and fountain created in 2009 visible from the road, along with commemorative trees and monuments. The lieutenant-governor's flag is flown from a flagpole in the grounds when he is present in the island. During the German occupation of the Channel Islands in the Second World War, the house was used as the residence of Generalleutnant Rudolf Graf von Schmettow, the German commandant. The 1989 issue of a £50 Jersey banknote featured an image of Government House on the reverse. Its coordinates are 49°11′41″N 2°05′40″W or 49.19486°N 2.09442°W.
